question: According to the manual, is stopping always the safest thing to do in an emergency?
choice_a: Yes, stopping is always safest
choice_b: Yes, unless the vehicle has ABS
choice_c: No, you should always leave the road instead
choice_d: No, when you don't have enough room to stop, you may have to steer away from what's ahead
explanation: The manual states stopping is not always the safest thing to do in an emergency. When you don't have enough room to stop, you may have to steer away from what's ahead.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.1 Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: Why can steering often help you avoid a crash better than braking?
choice_a: Because ABS only works while steering
choice_b: Because you can almost always turn to miss an obstacle more quickly than you can stop
choice_c: Because steering uses less fuel than braking
choice_d: Because brakes are unreliable on all commercial vehicles
explanation: The manual notes you can almost always turn to miss an obstacle more quickly than you can stop.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.1 Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: What caution does the manual give about steering quickly to avoid a crash?
choice_a: It requires ABS to be effective
choice_b: Top-heavy vehicles and tractors with multiple trailers may flip over
choice_c: It only works below 20 mph
choice_d: It is illegal in most states
explanation: The manual warns that top-heavy vehicles and tractors with multiple trailers may flip over when steering quickly.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.1 Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: Why should you keep both hands on the steering wheel at all times?
choice_a: In order to turn quickly in an emergency, you must have a firm grip on the wheel with both hands
choice_b: It prevents ABS malfunction
choice_c: It is required by federal regulation with no exceptions
choice_d: It keeps the parking brake engaged
explanation: The manual states that in order to turn quickly, you must have a firm grip on the steering wheel with both hands, so the best way is to keep them there all the time.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.1 Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: What is the recommended technique for returning to the paved road after leaving it, or for getting back on the road quickly?
choice_a: Hold the wheel tightly and turn sharply enough to get right back on the road safely, making it a single steer-counter-steer move
choice_b: Edge back gradually so tires don't grab
choice_c: Accelerate hard before turning the wheel
choice_d: Apply the parking brake first
explanation: The manual instructs to hold the wheel tightly and turn sharply, not edge gradually back onto the road since tires might grab unexpectedly and cause loss of control. The two turns should be made as a single steer-counter-steer move.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.1 Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: Why does the manual say edging gradually back onto the road is dangerous?
choice_a: It triggers the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_b: Your tires might grab unexpectedly and you could lose control
choice_c: It is against the law
choice_d: It wastes time in an emergency
explanation: If you edge gradually back onto the road, your tires might grab unexpectedly and you could lose control.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.1 Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: If you are blocked by traffic on both sides and must choose a direction, why might moving to the right be the best choice?
choice_a: Right turns require less steering input
choice_b: It keeps you closer to an escape ramp
choice_c: It is always faster
choice_d: At least you won't force anyone into an opposing traffic lane and a possible head-on collision
explanation: The manual explains that moving right avoids forcing anyone into an opposing traffic lane and a possible head-on collision.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.1 Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: According to the manual, can most shoulders support the weight of a large vehicle if you must leave the road?
choice_a: No, shoulders are never strong enough
choice_b: Only paved shoulders can support a large vehicle
choice_c: Yes, most shoulders are strong enough and offer an available escape route
choice_d: Only in dry weather
explanation: Most shoulders are strong enough to support the weight of a large vehicle and, therefore, offer an available escape route.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.1 Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: If you must drive off onto the shoulder, what braking guidance does the manual give?
choice_a: Never use the brakes on a shoulder
choice_b: Brake as hard as possible immediately
choice_c: Only use the parking brake
choice_d: Avoid using the brakes until your speed has dropped to about 20 mph, then brake very gently
explanation: If possible, avoid using the brakes until your speed has dropped to about 20 mph, then brake very gently to avoid skidding on a loose surface.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.1 Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: While on the shoulder, what helps you maintain control according to the manual?
choice_a: Turning the steering wheel back and forth
choice_b: Turning off the headlights
choice_c: Keeping one set of wheels on the pavement, if possible
choice_d: Shifting into neutral
explanation: Keeping one set of wheels on the pavement, if possible, helps to maintain control.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.1 Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: What should you do before pulling back onto the road after stopping on the shoulder?
choice_a: Signal and check your mirrors
choice_b: Nothing special, just accelerate
choice_c: Turn on your emergency flashers only
choice_d: Wait exactly 30 seconds
explanation: Stay on the shoulder until your vehicle has come to a stop, then signal and check your mirrors before pulling back onto the road.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.1 Steering to Avoid a Crash

question: What is the "controlled braking" method of stopping quickly?
choice_a: Using only the parking brake
choice_b: Releasing the brakes completely and coasting to a stop
choice_c: Pumping the brakes rapidly in short bursts
choice_d: Applying the brakes as hard as you can without locking the wheels, keeping steering movements very small
explanation: With controlled braking, you apply the brakes as hard as you can without locking the wheels, keeping steering wheel movements very small; if a larger adjustment is needed or the wheels lock, release the brakes and reapply as soon as you can.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.2 How to Stop Quickly and Safely

question: What is the "stab braking" method?
choice_a: Tapping the brake pedal lightly and repeatedly
choice_b: Braking only with the left front wheel
choice_c: Applying the parking brake and service brake at the same time
choice_d: Applying the brakes all the way, releasing when the wheels lock up, then applying fully again once wheels start rolling
explanation: With stab braking, you apply your brakes all the way, release the brakes when the wheels lock up, and as soon as the wheels start rolling, apply the brakes fully again.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.2 How to Stop Quickly and Safely

question: In stab braking, about how long can it take for the wheels to start rolling again after you release the brakes?
choice_a: Up to one second
choice_b: Instantly, with no delay
choice_c: Up to ten seconds
choice_d: Up to five seconds
explanation: It can take up to one second for the wheels to start rolling after you release the brakes; if you re-apply the brakes before the wheels start rolling, the vehicle won't straighten out.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.2 How to Stop Quickly and Safely

question: What happens if you jam on the brakes as hard as you can in an emergency?
choice_a: It automatically engages ABS on all vehicles
choice_b: It shifts the vehicle into a lower gear
choice_c: It will only keep the wheels locked up and cause a skid, and you cannot control the vehicle while skidding
choice_d: It stops the vehicle fastest with no downside
explanation: Emergency braking does not mean pushing the brake pedal as hard as you can; that will only keep the wheels locked up and cause a skid, and if the wheels are skidding, you cannot control the vehicle.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.2 How to Stop Quickly and Safely

question: What are the two most common causes of hydraulic brake failure discussed in the manual?
choice_a: Loss of hydraulic pressure and brake fade on long hills
choice_b: Worn tires and low fuel
choice_c: ABS malfunction and dead battery
choice_d: Overinflated tires and frozen brake lines
explanation: Most hydraulic brake failures occur for one of two reasons: loss of hydraulic pressure or brake fade on long hills.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: How does a loss of hydraulic pressure typically feel to the driver?
choice_a: The engine stalls immediately
choice_b: The brake pedal will feel spongy or go to the floor
choice_c: The steering wheel locks up
choice_d: The parking brake automatically releases
explanation: When the system won't build up pressure, the brake pedal will feel spongy or go to the floor.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: If you lose hydraulic brake pressure, what should you do to help slow the vehicle?
choice_a: Turn off the engine
choice_b: Shift into neutral
choice_c: Accelerate to bypass the failure
choice_d: Downshift into a lower gear
explanation: Downshifting the vehicle into a lower gear will help to slow the vehicle when hydraulic pressure is lost.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: How can pumping the brake pedal help after a loss of hydraulic pressure?
choice_a: It engages the engine retarder
choice_b: It activates the ABS system
choice_c: It generates enough hydraulic pressure to sometimes stop the vehicle
choice_d: It cools the brake drums
explanation: Sometimes pumping the brake pedal will generate enough hydraulic pressure to stop the vehicle.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: Why is the parking/emergency brake useful when hydraulic brakes fail?
choice_a: It is separate from the hydraulic brake system, so it can be used to slow the vehicle
choice_b: It is more powerful than the service brake
choice_c: It automatically restores hydraulic pressure
choice_d: It only works below 5 mph
explanation: The parking or emergency brake is separate from the hydraulic brake system and can therefore be used to slow the vehicle.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: When using the parking/emergency brake to slow a vehicle with failed hydraulic brakes, what should you do at the same time?
choice_a: Press the release button or pull the release lever to adjust brake pressure and keep the wheels from locking up
choice_b: Turn off the headlights
choice_c: Shift into reverse
choice_d: Open the driver's door
explanation: Be sure to press the release button or pull the release lever at the same time you use the emergency brake so you can adjust the brake pressure and keep the wheels from locking up.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: While slowing a vehicle with brake failure, what should you look for?
choice_a: A place to abandon the vehicle immediately
choice_b: An escape route such as an open field, side street, or escape ramp
choice_c: A gas station to pull into
choice_d: The nearest weigh station
explanation: While slowing the vehicle, look for an escape route -- an open field, side-street, or escape ramp.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: According to the manual, why is turning uphill a good way to slow and stop a vehicle with brake failure?
choice_a: It cools the tires
choice_b: It engages the ABS system
choice_c: It uses gravity to help slow and stop the vehicle
choice_d: It automatically restores braking power
explanation: Turning uphill is a good way to slow and stop the vehicle; you must also make sure it does not start rolling backward after you stop.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: After stopping a vehicle by turning uphill during a brake failure, what should you do to keep it from rolling backward?
choice_a: Put it in low gear, apply the parking brake, and if necessary roll back into an obstacle that will stop the vehicle
choice_b: Set out reflective triangles first
choice_c: Turn off the engine and leave it in neutral
choice_d: Open all doors
explanation: Make sure the vehicle does not start rolling backward after you stop. Put it in low gear, apply the parking brake, and, if necessary, roll back into some obstacle that will stop the vehicle.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: What will almost always prevent brake failure on long downgrades?
choice_a: Using the parking brake continuously
choice_b: Turning off the engine while coasting
choice_c: Going slow enough and braking properly
choice_d: Driving in the highest gear available
explanation: Going slow enough and braking properly will almost always prevent brake failure on long downgrades.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: If your brakes fail on a downgrade, what is described as your best hope?
choice_a: Driving into oncoming traffic's shoulder
choice_b: An escape ramp
choice_c: Shifting into reverse
choice_d: A U-turn
explanation: Once brakes have failed on a downgrade, your best hope is an escape ramp.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: Where are escape ramps usually located relative to a downgrade?
choice_a: Always exactly at the bottom of the downgrade
choice_b: Usually a few miles from the top of the downgrade
choice_c: Only at the very top of the downgrade
choice_d: Randomly placed with no relation to the downgrade
explanation: Ramps are usually located a few miles from the top of the downgrade, and there'll be signs telling you about them.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: How do some escape ramps bring a vehicle to a stop?
choice_a: Using an electric braking cable
choice_b: Using a steel net across the road
choice_c: Using soft gravel that resists the motion of the vehicle, sometimes combined with an uphill grade
choice_d: Using a large body of water
explanation: Some escape ramps use soft gravel that resists the motion of the vehicle and brings it to a stop; others turn uphill, using the hill to stop the vehicle and soft gravel to hold it in place.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: If no escape ramp is available after brake failure on a downgrade, what should you do?
choice_a: Drive into the opposing lane
choice_b: Take the least hazardous escape route available, such as an open field or a side road that flattens out or turns uphill
choice_c: Wait as long as possible before taking any action
choice_d: Turn off the engine and coast to the bottom
explanation: If no escape ramp is available, take the least hazardous escape route you can -- such as an open field or a side road that flattens out or turns uphill.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: Why does the manual say you should make your escape-route move as soon as you know your brakes don't work?
choice_a: It has no real effect on safety
choice_b: The longer you wait, the faster the vehicle will go, and the harder it will be to stop
choice_c: Escape ramps close after a set time
choice_d: Other drivers are required to yield only for the first ten seconds
explanation: Make the move as soon as you know your brakes don't work -- the longer you wait, the faster the vehicle will go, and the harder it will be to stop.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.3 Brake Failure

question: What is one major sign of tire failure described in the manual?
choice_a: The ABS lamp flashing
choice_b: The loud "bang" of a blowout
choice_c: The horn sounding automatically
choice_d: A sudden increase in fuel economy
explanation: The loud "bang" of a blowout is an easily recognized sign of tire failure.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.4 Tire Failure

question: If you hear a tire blow while driving, what should you assume?
choice_a: It is probably another vehicle's tire, not yours
choice_b: You'd be safest to assume it is yours
choice_c: It means the ABS has failed
choice_d: It is always just road debris
explanation: Any time you hear a tire blow, you'd be safest to assume it is yours, since it can take a few seconds for your vehicle to react.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.4 Tire Failure

question: What might heavy thumping or vibration while driving indicate?
choice_a: That the parking brake is engaged
choice_b: That the fuel tank is empty
choice_c: That one of the tires has gone flat
choice_d: That the ABS is working correctly
explanation: If the vehicle thumps or vibrates heavily, it may be a sign that one of the tires has gone flat; with a rear tire, that may be the only sign you get.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.4 Tire Failure

question: If the steering feels "heavy," what does that probably indicate?
choice_a: That one of the front tires has failed
choice_b: That the ABS has activated
choice_c: That the vehicle is overloaded in the rear
choice_d: That the trailer brakes have locked
explanation: If the steering feels "heavy," it is probably a sign that one of the front tires has failed.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.4 Tire Failure

question: What can happen when a rear tire fails, and what usually prevents this?
choice_a: The vehicle will always roll over, and only ABS prevents it
choice_b: The vehicle may slide back and forth or "fishtail," but dual rear tires usually prevent this
choice_c: Nothing happens; rear tire failure has no effect on handling
choice_d: The engine will stall, prevented by cruise control
explanation: Failure of a rear tire will sometimes cause the vehicle to slide back and forth or "fishtail"; however, dual rear tires usually prevent this.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.4 Tire Failure

question: If a front tire fails, why is it important to hold the steering wheel firmly with both hands?
choice_a: A failed front tire can twist the steering wheel out of your hand
choice_b: It automatically applies the parking brake
choice_c: It prevents the tire pressure warning light from coming on
choice_d: It is required by the manufacturer's warranty
explanation: If a front tire fails, it can twist the steering wheel out of your hand; the only way to prevent this is to keep a firm grip on the steering wheel with both hands at all times.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.4 Tire Failure

question: When a tire fails, why does the manual say to stay off the brake (unless about to run into something)?
choice_a: It is a legal requirement to coast to a stop
choice_b: The brakes will not work at all with a flat tire
choice_c: Braking when a tire has failed could cause loss of control
choice_d: Braking would overheat the ABS sensors
explanation: It's natural to want to brake in an emergency; however, braking when a tire has failed could cause loss of control. Stay off the brake until the vehicle has slowed, then brake gently, pull off the road, and stop.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.4 Tire Failure

question: After a tire failure and coming to a stop, what should you do even if the vehicle seems to be handling all right?
choice_a: Get out and check all the tires
choice_b: Replace the spare tire without checking others
choice_c: Immediately continue driving to the next town
choice_d: Call for a tow truck without inspecting anything
explanation: After you've come to a stop, get out and check all the tires, even if the vehicle seems to be handling all right -- if one of your dual tires goes, the only way you may know it is by getting out and looking at it.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.17.4 Tire Failure

question: What is ABS?
choice_a: A cruise control override system
choice_b: A device that automatically applies the parking brake
choice_c: A computerized system that keeps your wheels from locking up during hard brake applications
choice_d: A backup fuel injection system
explanation: ABS is a computerized system that keeps your wheels from locking up during hard brake applications.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18 Antilock Braking Systems

question: Does ABS increase or decrease your normal braking capability?
choice_a: It decreases braking capability on dry pavement
choice_b: It does not decrease or increase your normal braking capability; it only activates when wheels are about to lock up
choice_c: It significantly increases stopping power in all situations
choice_d: It replaces the normal brakes entirely
explanation: ABS is an addition to your normal brakes. It does not decrease or increase your normal braking capability. ABS only activates when wheels are about to lock up.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18 Antilock Braking Systems

question: Does ABS necessarily shorten your stopping distance?
choice_a: Yes, but only on wet roads
choice_b: No, but it does help you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking
choice_c: No, it has no effect on braking at all
choice_d: Yes, it always shortens stopping distance significantly
explanation: ABS does not necessarily shorten your stopping distance, but it does help you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18 Antilock Braking Systems

question: How does ABS work?
choice_a: It increases engine RPM to slow the drive wheels
choice_b: It disconnects the trailer brakes automatically
choice_c: It releases air from the tires to increase traction
choice_d: Sensors detect potential wheel lockup and an electronic control unit (ECU) decreases brake pressure to avoid lockup
explanation: Sensors detect potential wheel lock up. An electronic control unit (ECU) will then decrease brake pressure to avoid wheel lockup.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.1 How Antilock Braking Systems Work

question: How is brake pressure adjusted by an ABS-equipped vehicle?
choice_a: It is increased until the wheels lock
choice_b: It is reduced to a fixed 50% of normal pressure
choice_c: It is turned off completely once activated
choice_d: It is adjusted to provide the maximum braking without danger of lockup
explanation: Brake pressure is adjusted to provide the maximum braking without danger of lockup.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.1 How Antilock Braking Systems Work

question: How does ABS's reaction speed compare to a driver's?
choice_a: ABS is slower than a driver's reaction time
choice_b: They react at exactly the same speed
choice_c: ABS only reacts after the driver releases the brake
choice_d: ABS works far faster than the driver can respond to potential wheel lockup
explanation: ABS works far faster than the driver can respond to potential wheel lockup. At all other times the brake system will operate normally.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.1 How Antilock Braking Systems Work

question: Truck tractors with air brakes built on or after what date are required to have ABS?
choice_a: March 1, 1999
choice_b: January 1, 2000
choice_c: March 1, 1998
choice_d: March 1, 1997
explanation: The Department of Transportation requires that ABS be on truck tractors with air brakes built on or after March 1, 1997.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.2 Vehicles Required to Have Antilock Braking Systems

question: Other air brake vehicles (trucks, buses, trailers, and converter dollies) are required to have ABS if built on or after what date?
choice_a: March 1, 2000
choice_b: March 1, 1999
choice_c: March 1, 1997
choice_d: March 1, 1998
explanation: Other air brake vehicles (trucks, buses, trailers, and converter dollies) built on or after March 1, 1998 are required to have ABS.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.2 Vehicles Required to Have Antilock Braking Systems

question: Hydraulically braked trucks and buses with what gross vehicle weight rating built on or after March 1, 1999 are required to have ABS?
choice_a: 8,000 lbs or more
choice_b: 5,000 lbs or more
choice_c: 10,000 lbs or more
choice_d: 26,000 lbs or more
explanation: Hydraulically braked trucks and buses with a gross vehicle weight rating of 10,000 lbs or more built on or after March 1, 1999 are required to have ABS.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.2 Vehicles Required to Have Antilock Braking Systems

question: Where are ABS malfunction lamps located on tractors, trucks, and buses?
choice_a: There is no dashboard lamp; you must check under the vehicle
choice_b: Inside the glove compartment
choice_c: On the instrument panel, and they are yellow
choice_d: On the rear bumper only
explanation: Tractors, trucks, and buses will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the instrument panel.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.3 How to Know If Your Vehicle Is Equipped with ABS

question: Where are ABS malfunction lamps located on trailers?
choice_a: Red lamps on the right side only
choice_b: On the instrument panel like a tractor
choice_c: Trailers never have malfunction lamps
choice_d: Yellow lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner
explanation: Trailers will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.3 How to Know If Your Vehicle Is Equipped with ABS

question: Dollies manufactured on or after what date are required to have an ABS lamp on the left side?
choice_a: March 1, 1998
choice_b: March 1, 1997
choice_c: January 1, 1998
choice_d: March 1, 1999
explanation: Dollies manufactured on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have a lamp on the left side.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.3 How to Know If Your Vehicle Is Equipped with ABS

question: On newer vehicles, how does the ABS malfunction lamp behave at start-up?
choice_a: It never illuminates unless there is a fault
choice_b: It flashes continuously until the engine reaches operating temperature
choice_c: It comes on for a bulb check, then goes out quickly
choice_d: It stays on for the entire trip
explanation: As a system check on newer vehicles, the malfunction lamp comes on at start-up for a bulb check, and then goes out quickly.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.3 How to Know If Your Vehicle Is Equipped with ABS

question: On older ABS systems, how long could the malfunction lamp stay on during the bulb check?
choice_a: Until the engine is turned off
choice_b: For exactly ten minutes
choice_c: Until you are driving over five mph
choice_d: It never turns off on older systems
explanation: On older systems, the lamp could stay on until you are driving over five mph.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.3 How to Know If Your Vehicle Is Equipped with ABS

question: What does it mean if the ABS malfunction lamp stays on after the bulb check, or comes on once you are under way?
choice_a: You may have lost ABS control
choice_b: The parking brake is engaged
choice_c: The vehicle is overloaded
choice_d: The system is functioning perfectly
explanation: If the lamp stays on after the bulb check, or goes on once you are under way, you may have lost ABS control.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.3 How to Know If Your Vehicle Is Equipped with ABS

question: For a towed unit manufactured before ABS was required, how can you tell if it has ABS if it may be difficult to tell otherwise?
choice_a: Look under the vehicle for the ECU and wheel speed sensor wires coming from the back of the brakes
choice_b: Look at the manufacturer's sticker on the dashboard only
choice_c: There is no way to tell
choice_d: Check the tire pressure
explanation: In the case of towed units manufactured before ABS was required, look under the vehicle for the ECU and wheel speed sensor wires coming from the back of the brakes.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.3 How to Know If Your Vehicle Is Equipped with ABS

question: Without ABS, what happens when you brake hard on slippery surfaces and your steering wheels lock up?
choice_a: The vehicle stops faster
choice_b: You lose steering control
choice_c: Nothing changes
choice_d: Fuel efficiency improves
explanation: When your steering wheels lock up, you lose steering control.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.4 How ABS Helps You

question: Without ABS, what can happen when your other (non-steering) wheels lock up while braking hard?
choice_a: The vehicle automatically shifts to a lower gear
choice_b: The vehicle accelerates unexpectedly
choice_c: The parking brake engages
choice_d: You may skid, jackknife, or even spin the vehicle
explanation: When your other wheels lock up, you may skid, jackknife, or even spin the vehicle.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.4 How ABS Helps You

question: What benefit does ABS provide even if it may not stop you faster?
choice_a: It eliminates the need for a parking brake
choice_b: It permanently increases tire tread depth
choice_c: It should let you steer around an obstacle while braking and avoid skids caused by over braking
choice_d: It reduces fuel consumption
explanation: You may or may not be able to stop faster with ABS, but you should be able to steer around an obstacle while braking, and avoid skids caused by over braking.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.4 How ABS Helps You

question: If only the tractor has ABS (not the trailer), what should you do if the trailer begins to swing out?
choice_a: Apply the brakes harder immediately
choice_b: Turn the steering wheel sharply toward the swing
choice_c: Let up on the brakes (if you can safely do so)
choice_d: Accelerate to straighten the trailer
explanation: When only the tractor has ABS, you should be able to maintain steering control and there is less chance of jackknifing, but keep your eye on the trailer and let up on the brakes if it begins to swing out.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.5 ABS on the Tractor Only or Only on the Trailer

question: If only the trailer has ABS and you lose steering control or start a tractor jackknife, what should you do?
choice_a: Let up on the brakes (if you can safely do so) until you regain control
choice_b: Apply full brake pressure
choice_c: Turn the steering wheel as far as possible in one direction
choice_d: Shift into a higher gear
explanation: When only the trailer has ABS, the trailer is less likely to swing out, but if you lose steering control or start a tractor jackknife, let up on the brakes until you regain control.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.5 ABS on the Tractor Only or Only on the Trailer

question: How should you brake if you drive a vehicle equipped with ABS?
choice_a: Always brake as hard as possible from the first touch of the pedal
choice_b: Brake as you always have, using only the braking force necessary to stop safely and stay in control
choice_c: Pump the brakes rapidly regardless of conditions
choice_d: Avoid using the brakes and rely on downshifting instead
explanation: When you drive a vehicle with ABS, you should brake as you always have, using only the braking force necessary to stop safely and stay in control.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.6 Braking with ABS

question: What is the one exception where you can fully apply the brakes in an emergency stop with ABS?
choice_a: Only when driving below 30 mph
choice_b: Whenever the road is dry
choice_c: If you drive a straight truck or combination with working ABS on all axles
choice_d: Only on bridges
explanation: There is only one exception to the normal ABS braking procedure: if you drive a straight truck or combination with working ABS on all axles, in an emergency stop, you can fully apply the brakes.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.6 Braking with ABS

question: If your ABS malfunctions, what should you do?
choice_a: Drive normally, since you still have regular brakes, but get the system serviced soon
choice_b: Drive only in reverse until repaired
choice_c: Disconnect the trailer
choice_d: Stop the vehicle immediately and abandon it
explanation: If your ABS malfunctions, you still have regular brakes. Drive normally, but get the system serviced soon.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.7 Braking If ABS Is Not Working

question: Which of the following is a true safety reminder about ABS according to the manual?
choice_a: ABS allows you to follow more closely since it stops you faster
choice_b: ABS eliminates the need for safe following distance
choice_c: ABS won't allow you to drive faster, follow more closely, or drive less carefully
choice_d: ABS lets you drive safely regardless of road conditions
explanation: ABS won't allow you to drive faster, follow more closely, or drive less carefully.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.8 Safety Reminders

question: What kinds of skids will ABS NOT prevent?
choice_a: Skids caused only by rain
choice_b: Skids on ice specifically
choice_c: Power or turning skids caused by spinning the drive wheels or going too fast in a turn
choice_d: All skids of every kind
explanation: ABS won't prevent power or turning skids -- ABS should prevent brake-induced skids or jackknifes, but not those caused by spinning the drive wheels or going too fast in a turn.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.8 Safety Reminders

question: According to the safety reminders, is ABS a replacement for your normal brakes?
choice_a: ABS replaces the parking brake only
choice_b: No, ABS is an "add-on" to your normal brakes, not a replacement for them
choice_c: Yes, but only on trailers
choice_d: Yes, ABS entirely replaces the service brake system
explanation: ABS won't increase or decrease ultimate stopping power -- ABS is an "add-on" to your normal brakes, not a replacement for them.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.8 Safety Reminders

question: Will ABS compensate for bad brakes or poor brake maintenance?
choice_a: Yes, ABS is designed specifically to fix worn brakes
choice_b: It compensates fully but only in dry conditions
choice_c: No, ABS won't compensate for bad brakes or poor brake maintenance
choice_d: Yes, but only for the front axle
explanation: ABS won't compensate for bad brakes or poor brake maintenance.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.8 Safety Reminders

question: According to the manual's safety reminders, what is still the best vehicle safety feature?
choice_a: The parking brake
choice_b: The escape ramp
choice_c: A safe driver
choice_d: The ABS system itself
explanation: Remember: The best vehicle safety feature is still a safe driver.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.18.8 Safety Reminders

question: What happens whenever a skid occurs?
choice_a: The ABS system deactivates completely
choice_b: The transmission locks
choice_c: The tires lose their grip on the road
choice_d: The engine automatically shuts off
explanation: A skid happens whenever the tires lose their grip on the road.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19 Skid Control and Recovery

question: What are the four ways skids are caused, according to the manual?
choice_a: Overloading, underinflation, wheel imbalance, and worn brakes
choice_b: Rain, snow, ice, and fog
choice_c: Over-braking, over-steering, over-acceleration, and driving too fast
choice_d: ABS failure, engine failure, tire failure, and steering failure
explanation: A skid is caused in one of four ways: over-braking, over-steering, over-acceleration, and driving too fast.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19 Skid Control and Recovery

question: Besides braking too hard and locking up the wheels, what else can cause an over-braking skid?
choice_a: Using cruise control on the highway
choice_b: Downshifting too early
choice_c: Turning on the headlights
choice_d: Using the speed retarder when the road is slippery
explanation: Over-braking is braking too hard and locking up the wheels. Skids also can occur when using the speed retarder when the road is slippery.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19 Skid Control and Recovery

question: What is "over-steering" as a cause of a skid?
choice_a: Turning the wheel too slowly
choice_b: Failing to signal before turning
choice_c: Steering with only one hand
choice_d: Turning the wheels more sharply than the vehicle can turn
explanation: Over-steering is turning the wheels more sharply than the vehicle can turn.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19 Skid Control and Recovery

question: What is "over-acceleration" as a cause of a skid?
choice_a: Driving faster than the posted speed limit
choice_b: Using the engine brake on a downgrade
choice_c: Supplying too much power to the drive wheels, causing them to spin
choice_d: Accelerating out of a parking spot
explanation: Over-acceleration is supplying too much power to the drive wheels, causing them to spin.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19 Skid Control and Recovery

question: What does the manual say is the cause of most serious skids?
choice_a: Using the horn excessively
choice_b: Worn windshield wipers
choice_c: Driving too fast for road conditions
choice_d: Overinflated tires
explanation: Most serious skids result from driving too fast for road conditions. Drivers who adjust their driving to conditions don't over-accelerate and don't have to over-brake or over-steer from too much speed.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19 Skid Control and Recovery

question: What is the most common type of skid described in the manual?
choice_a: One in which the front wheels spin freely
choice_b: A skid caused by a steering wheel malfunction
choice_c: One in which the rear wheels lose traction through excessive braking or acceleration
choice_d: A skid caused by an overinflated tire
explanation: By far the most common skid is one in which the rear wheels lose traction through excessive braking or acceleration.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.1 Drive-wheel Skids

question: Skids caused by acceleration usually happen under what conditions, and how can you easily stop them?
choice_a: Usually on dry pavement; applying the brakes hard stops them
choice_b: Usually on ice or snow; taking your foot off the accelerator can easily stop them
choice_c: Usually in heavy rain; turning the steering wheel sharply stops them
choice_d: Usually at low speed; honking the horn stops them
explanation: Skids caused by acceleration usually happen on ice or snow. Taking your foot off the accelerator can easily stop them.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.1 Drive-wheel Skids

question: If it is very slippery during an acceleration skid, what additional action does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Push the clutch in, otherwise the engine can keep the wheels from rolling freely and regaining traction
choice_b: Shift into the highest gear available
choice_c: Turn off the engine completely
choice_d: Apply the parking brake fully
explanation: If it is very slippery, push the clutch in. Otherwise, the engine can keep the wheels from rolling freely and regaining traction.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.1 Drive-wheel Skids

question: What happens during a rear-wheel braking skid, and why?
choice_a: The rear wheels lock and slide sideways in an attempt to "catch up" with the front wheels, because locked wheels have less traction than rolling wheels
choice_b: The trailer detaches from the tractor
choice_c: The front wheels lock and the vehicle stops immediately
choice_d: The engine stalls and the vehicle rolls backward
explanation: Rear wheel braking skids occur when the rear drive wheels lock. Because locked wheels have less traction than rolling wheels, the rear wheels usually slide sideways in an attempt to "catch up" with the front wheels.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.1 Drive-wheel Skids

question: In a bus or straight truck, what does a drive-wheel braking skid typically cause?
choice_a: The vehicle will accelerate uncontrollably
choice_b: The vehicle will flip forward
choice_c: The vehicle will slide sideways in a "spin out"
choice_d: The vehicle will roll to a smooth stop
explanation: In a bus or straight truck, the vehicle will slide sideways in a "spin out" during a drive-wheel braking skid.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.1 Drive-wheel Skids

question: With vehicles towing trailers, what can a drive-wheel skid cause?
choice_a: The tractor will accelerate on its own
choice_b: The trailer will automatically detach
choice_c: The trailer can push the towing vehicle sideways, causing a sudden jackknife
choice_d: The trailer brakes will fail permanently
explanation: With vehicles towing trailers, a drive-wheel skid can let the trailer push the towing vehicle sideways, causing a sudden jackknife.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.1 Drive-wheel Skids

question: What is the first step to correct a drive-wheel braking skid?
choice_a: Accelerate to regain traction
choice_b: Apply the brakes even harder
choice_c: Stop braking, which lets the rear wheels roll again and keeps them from sliding
choice_d: Turn the steering wheel as far as it will go
explanation: To correct a drive-wheel braking skid: Stop Braking. This will let the rear wheels roll again, and keep the rear wheels from sliding.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.2 Correcting a Drive-wheel Braking Skid

question: Why must you counter-steer when correcting a skid, according to the manual?
choice_a: It keeps the parking brake from engaging
choice_b: As a vehicle turns back on course it has a tendency to keep on turning, so unless you turn the wheel quickly the other way, you may skid in the opposite direction
choice_c: Counter-steering increases braking power
choice_d: It is required to reset the ABS system
explanation: As a vehicle turns back on course, it has a tendency to keep on turning. Unless you turn the steering wheel quickly the other way, you may find yourself skidding in the opposite direction.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.2 Correcting a Drive-wheel Braking Skid

question: Where does the manual say is the best place to practice skid recovery skills?
choice_a: A residential neighborhood at night
choice_b: A busy public highway
choice_c: An icy parking lot with other traffic present
choice_d: A large driving range or "skid pad"
explanation: Learning to stay off the brake, turn the steering wheel quickly, push in the clutch, and counter-steer in a skid takes a lot of practice. The best place to get this practice is on a large driving range or "skid pad."
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.2 Correcting a Drive-wheel Braking Skid

question: What causes most front-wheel skids?
choice_a: Overinflated rear tires
choice_b: A malfunctioning ABS sensor on the rear axle
choice_c: Using the parking brake while moving
choice_d: Driving too fast for conditions
explanation: Driving too fast for conditions causes most front-wheel skids.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.3 Front-wheel Skids

question: Besides driving too fast, what other causes of front-wheel skids does the manual list?
choice_a: Excessive following distance
choice_b: A dirty windshield and worn wiper blades
choice_c: Lack of tread on the front tires and cargo loaded so not enough weight is on the front axle
choice_d: Using the engine brake and low tire pressure in the rear
explanation: Other causes include lack of tread on the front tires and cargo loaded so not enough weight is on the front axle.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.3 Front-wheel Skids

question: In a front-wheel skid, what happens to the front end of the vehicle regardless of how much you turn the steering wheel?
choice_a: It tends to go in a straight line
choice_b: It reverses direction
choice_c: It spins in a complete circle
choice_d: It turns sharply in the direction of steering input
explanation: In a front-wheel skid, the front end tends to go in a straight line regardless of how much you turn the steering wheel.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.3 Front-wheel Skids

question: What is the only way to stop a front-wheel skid?
choice_a: Accelerate to regain front tire traction
choice_b: Apply the parking brake immediately
choice_c: Turn the steering wheel as sharply as possible
choice_d: Let the vehicle slow down by stopping turning and/or braking so hard, slowing as quickly as possible without skidding
explanation: When a front-wheel skid occurs, the only way to stop the skid is to let the vehicle slow down. Stop turning and/or braking so hard. Slow down as quickly as possible without skidding.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.19.3 Front-wheel Skids

question: What are the three basic steps to take at any accident, according to the manual?
choice_a: Turn off the engine, remove cargo, and wait for a tow truck
choice_b: Call your dispatcher, take photos, and exchange insurance information
choice_c: Protect the area, notify authorities, and care for the injured
choice_d: Move all vehicles immediately, direct traffic, and file a police report
explanation: The basic steps to be taken at any accident are to: protect the area, notify authorities, and care for the injured.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20 Accident Procedures

question: What is the first thing to do at an accident scene, according to the manual?
choice_a: Move all vehicles off the roadway immediately regardless of safety
choice_b: Exchange contact information with the other driver
choice_c: Call your insurance company
choice_d: Keep another accident from happening in the same spot
explanation: The first thing to do at an accident scene is to keep another accident from happening in the same spot.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20.1 Protect the Area

question: If your vehicle is involved in an accident, what should you try to do to protect the area?
choice_a: Leave it exactly where it stopped, blocking the lane
choice_b: Push it into the opposing lane
choice_c: Immediately unload all cargo onto the roadway
choice_d: Try to get it to the side of the road to prevent another accident and allow traffic to move
explanation: If your vehicle is involved in the accident, try to get it to the side of the road; this will help prevent another accident and allow traffic to move.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20.1 Protect the Area

question: If you're stopping to help at an accident you weren't involved in, where should you park?
choice_a: As close as possible to get a better view
choice_b: In the opposing traffic lane
choice_c: Directly behind the damaged vehicle
choice_d: Away from the accident, since the area immediately around it will be needed for emergency vehicles
explanation: If you're stopping to help, park away from the accident. The area immediately around the accident will be needed for emergency vehicles.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20.1 Protect the Area

question: What should you set out to warn other traffic of an accident?
choice_a: A fire extinguisher
choice_b: Reflective triangles, positioned so other drivers can see them in time to avoid the accident
choice_c: Your shipping papers
choice_d: Nothing; flashers alone are always sufficient
explanation: Set out reflective triangles to warn other traffic. Make sure other drivers can see them in time to avoid the accident.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20.1 Protect the Area

question: If you have a cell phone or CB at an accident scene, when should you call for assistance?
choice_a: Never; wait for another driver to call
choice_b: Before you get out of your vehicle
choice_c: Only after protecting the scene and caring for the injured
choice_d: Only if someone is unconscious
explanation: If you have a cell phone or CB, call for assistance before you get out of your vehicle.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20.2 Notify Authorities

question: If you do not have a cell phone or CB, when should you phone or send someone to phone the police?
choice_a: You should never call the police for a minor accident
choice_b: Immediately, even before protecting the scene
choice_c: Only if there are injuries
choice_d: After the accident scene has been properly protected
explanation: If you don't have a phone, wait until after the accident scene has been properly protected, then phone or send someone to phone the police.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20.2 Notify Authorities

question: When notifying authorities about an accident, what should you try to determine?
choice_a: Where you are, so you can give the exact location
choice_b: The make and model of the other vehicle only
choice_c: The other driver's insurance company
choice_d: The weather forecast for the next hour
explanation: Try to determine where you are so you can give the exact location.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20.2 Notify Authorities

question: If a qualified person is already at the accident helping the injured, what should you do?
choice_a: Leave the scene immediately
choice_b: Move the injured person to a more comfortable position
choice_c: Stay out of the way unless asked to assist
choice_d: Insist on taking over first aid duties
explanation: If a qualified person is at the accident and helping the injured, stay out of the way unless asked to assist.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20.3 Care for the Injured

question: When should you avoid moving a severely injured person?
choice_a: You should always move them to the shoulder immediately
choice_b: Moving injured persons is never appropriate under any circumstance
choice_c: Only if they ask to be moved
choice_d: Unless the danger of fire or passing traffic makes it necessary
explanation: Don't move a severely injured person unless the danger of fire or passing traffic makes it necessary.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20.3 Care for the Injured

question: How should you stop heavy bleeding on an injured person?
choice_a: By giving them water to drink
choice_b: By applying direct pressure to the wound
choice_c: By elevating their head only
choice_d: By applying ice directly to the wound
explanation: Stop heavy bleeding by applying direct pressure to the wound.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20.3 Care for the Injured

question: Besides controlling bleeding, what other simple step does the manual recommend for helping injured parties?
choice_a: Keep the injured person warm
choice_b: Have them stand up and walk around
choice_c: Give them food immediately
choice_d: Remove their protective clothing
explanation: Keep the injured person warm.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.20.3 Care for the Injured

question: According to the manual, what after-accident causes contribute to vehicle fires?
choice_a: Spilled fuel and improper use of flares
choice_b: Cold weather and low humidity
choice_c: Overinflated tires and clean electrical systems
choice_d: Proper cargo ventilation
explanation: Among the causes of vehicle fires listed: after accidents, spilled fuel and improper use of flares.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.1 Causes of Fire

question: What tire-related conditions can cause fires, according to the manual?
choice_a: Under-inflated tires and duals that touch
choice_b: Overinflated tires and new tread
choice_c: Cold tires in winter conditions
choice_d: Properly inflated tires with adequate clearance
explanation: Tire-related causes of fire include under-inflated tires and duals that touch.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.1 Causes of Fire

question: What electrical system issues can cause vehicle fires?
choice_a: Properly grounded circuits
choice_b: Short circuits due to damaged insulation and loose connections
choice_c: A fully charged battery
choice_d: New wiring harnesses
explanation: Electrical system causes of fire include short circuits due to damaged insulation and loose connections.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.1 Causes of Fire

question: What fuel-related behaviors does the manual list as causes of vehicle fires?
choice_a: Driver smoking, improper fueling, and loose fuel connections
choice_b: Parking near a fuel station
choice_c: Using a fuel additive
choice_d: Filling the tank completely
explanation: Fuel-related causes of fire include driver smoking, improper fueling, and loose fuel connections.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.1 Causes of Fire

question: What cargo-related factors can cause vehicle fires?
choice_a: Cargo that is too light
choice_b: Cargo secured with tie-downs
choice_c: Well-ventilated, properly sealed cargo
choice_d: Flammable cargo, improperly sealed or loaded cargo, and poor ventilation
explanation: Cargo-related causes of fire include flammable cargo, improperly sealed or loaded cargo, and poor ventilation.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.1 Causes of Fire

question: As part of fire prevention, what should a complete vehicle inspection cover?
choice_a: Only the cargo manifest
choice_b: Only the mirrors and lights
choice_c: Only the tires
choice_d: The electrical, fuel, and exhaust systems, tires, and cargo, and checking that the fire extinguisher is charged
explanation: Vehicle Inspection for fire prevention: make a complete inspection of the electrical, fuel, and exhaust systems, tires, and cargo; be sure the fire extinguisher is charged.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.2 Fire Prevention

question: During an en route inspection, what should you check for signs of heat whenever you stop during a trip?
choice_a: The tires, wheels, and truck body
choice_b: Only the windshield wipers
choice_c: Only the horn
choice_d: Only the mirrors
explanation: En Route Inspection: check the tires, wheels, and truck body for signs of heat whenever you stop during a trip.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.2 Fire Prevention

question: While driving, what should you monitor to help prevent fires?
choice_a: The GPS navigation screen only
choice_b: Only the speedometer
choice_c: Only the radio
choice_d: The instruments and gauges for overheating, and the mirrors for signs of smoke
explanation: Monitoring: check the instruments and gauges often for signs of overheating and use the mirrors to look for signs of smoke from tires or the vehicle.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.2 Fire Prevention

question: According to the manual, what mistake have drivers who didn't know what to do sometimes made regarding fires?
choice_a: They have made fires worse
choice_b: They alerted authorities too quickly
choice_c: They always successfully extinguished them anyway
choice_d: They over-prepared with too many extinguishers
explanation: Knowing how to fight fires is important. Drivers who didn't know what to do have made fires worse.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: When pulling off the road because of a vehicle fire, where should you park?
choice_a: Under a bridge for cover
choice_b: In an open area, away from buildings, trees, brush, other vehicles, or anything that might catch fire
choice_c: As close as possible to a service station
choice_d: In a parking garage
explanation: Park in an open area, away from buildings, trees, brush, other vehicles, or anything that might catch fire.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: What does the manual explicitly warn you not to do when your vehicle is on fire?
choice_a: Don't set the parking brake
choice_b: Don't pull into a service station
choice_c: Don't notify emergency services
choice_d: Don't turn off the engine
explanation: In pulling off the road due to fire: don't pull into a service station!
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: With an engine fire, what should you do regarding the hood?
choice_a: Remove the hood completely
choice_b: Leave the hood open while driving
choice_c: Open it immediately to check the damage
choice_d: Don't open the hood if you can avoid it
explanation: With an engine fire, turn off the engine as soon as you can. Don't open the hood if you can avoid it.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: How should you apply foam to fight an engine fire?
choice_a: Shoot foam through louvers, radiator, or from the vehicle's underside
choice_b: Spray it only on the tires
choice_c: Pour it directly on top of the hood
choice_d: Apply it to the windshield
explanation: For an engine fire: shoot foam through louvers, radiator, or from the vehicle's underside.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: For a cargo fire in a van or box trailer, especially with hazardous materials, what should you do with the doors?
choice_a: Open the doors immediately to let smoke escape
choice_b: Remove the doors entirely
choice_c: Keep the doors shut, because opening them supplies the fire with oxygen and can cause it to burn very fast
choice_d: It doesn't matter whether the doors are open or shut
explanation: For a cargo fire in a van or box trailer, keep the doors shut, especially if your cargo contains hazardous materials. Opening the van doors will supply the fire with oxygen and can cause it to burn very fast.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: When using a fire extinguisher, where should you aim?
choice_a: At the smoke
choice_b: It doesn't matter as long as you spray something
choice_c: At the source or base of the fire, not up in the flames
choice_d: Directly up into the flames
explanation: Aim at the source or base of the fire, not up in the flames.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: What type of fire is a B:C type fire extinguisher designed to work on?
choice_a: Only cloth fires
choice_b: Only combustible metal fires
choice_c: Electrical fires and burning liquids
choice_d: Only wood and paper fires
explanation: The B:C type fire extinguisher is designed to work on electrical fires and burning liquids.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: What additional fires can an A:B:C type extinguisher handle beyond what a B:C type handles?
choice_a: Nothing additional; A:B:C and B:C are identical
choice_b: Burning wood, paper, and cloth
choice_c: Only combustible metals
choice_d: Only radioactive material fires
explanation: The A:B:C type is designed to work on burning wood, paper, and cloth as well as electrical fires and burning liquids.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: Why should you not use water on an electrical fire?
choice_a: It will make the fire spread wood ash
choice_b: It can cause shock
choice_c: It has no effect either way
choice_d: Water is flammable
explanation: Water can be used on wood, paper, or cloth, but don't use water on an electrical fire because it can cause shock.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: Why should you not use water on a gasoline fire?
choice_a: It evaporates too quickly to help
choice_b: Gasoline fires cannot be extinguished by any method
choice_c: It will spread the flames
choice_d: It causes an electrical shock hazard
explanation: Don't use water on a gasoline fire -- it will spread the flames.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: How should a burning tire be handled?
choice_a: It should be left to burn out on its own
choice_b: It must be cooled, and lots of water may be required
choice_c: It should be removed from the vehicle while still burning
choice_d: It should be smothered with dry chemical only, never water
explanation: A burning tire must be cooled. Lots of water may be required.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: If you are unsure what extinguishing agent to use, especially on a hazardous materials fire, what should you do?
choice_a: Pour any available liquid on it
choice_b: Use water regardless of the risk
choice_c: Wait for firefighters
choice_d: Attempt to move the burning cargo away by hand
explanation: If you're not sure what to use, especially on a hazardous materials fire, wait for firefighters.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: When fighting a fire, where should you position yourself relative to the wind?
choice_a: Upwind, letting the wind carry the extinguisher agent to the fire
choice_b: Wind direction does not matter
choice_c: Directly in the smoke plume
choice_d: Downwind, so the smoke blows away from the fire
explanation: Position yourself upwind. Let the wind carry the extinguisher to the fire.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: Does the absence of smoke or flame mean a fire cannot restart?
choice_a: It depends solely on the extinguisher type used
choice_b: Yes, but only for electrical fires
choice_c: No, absence of smoke or flame does not mean the fire cannot restart
choice_d: Yes, once smoke and flame are gone the fire is permanently out
explanation: Continue until whatever was burning has been cooled. Absence of smoke or flame does not mean the fire cannot restart.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting

question: According to the fire class chart, what is a Class A fire and how is it extinguished?
choice_a: Wood, paper, and ordinary combustibles, extinguished by cooling and quenching using water or dry chemicals
choice_b: Combustible metal fires, extinguished with water
choice_c: Electrical equipment fires, extinguished with water
choice_d: Gasoline and other greasy liquids, extinguished with foam only
explanation: Class A fires (wood, paper, ordinary combustibles) are extinguished by cooling and quenching using water or dry chemicals.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting, Class/Type of Fires chart (Figure 2.20)

question: According to the fire class chart, what is a Class B fire and how is it extinguished?
choice_a: Electrical fires, extinguished with water
choice_b: Combustible metals, extinguished with specialized powders
choice_c: Wood and paper fires, extinguished with water only
choice_d: Gasoline, oil, grease, and other greasy liquids, extinguished by smothering, cooling, or heat shielding using carbon dioxide or dry chemicals
explanation: Class B fires (gasoline, oil, grease, other greasy liquids) are extinguished by smothering, cooling, or heat shielding using carbon dioxide or dry chemicals.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting, Class/Type of Fires chart (Figure 2.20)

question: According to the fire class chart, how should a Class C (electrical equipment) fire be extinguished?
choice_a: With non-conducting agents such as carbon dioxide or dry chemicals; do NOT use water
choice_b: With water only
choice_c: With any liquid available
choice_d: With foam only
explanation: Class C fires (electrical equipment fires) are extinguished with non-conducting agents such as carbon dioxide or dry chemicals; the chart explicitly states DO NOT USE WATER.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting, Class/Type of Fires chart (Figure 2.20)

question: According to the fire class chart, how is a Class D fire (combustible metals) extinguished?
choice_a: With plain water
choice_b: With foam
choice_c: By using specialized extinguishing powders
choice_d: With carbon dioxide only
explanation: Class D fires (fires in combustible metals) are extinguished by using specialized extinguishing powders.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.21.3 Fire Fighting, Class/Type of Fires chart (Figure 2.20)

question: According to the class-of-fire/extinguisher-type table, which extinguisher type is rated for Classes A, B, C, or D?
choice_a: KCL Dry Chemical
choice_b: Multi-Purpose Dry Chemical
choice_c: Water With Anti-Freeze
choice_d: Purple K Dry Chemical
explanation: The table lists Multi-Purpose Dry Chemical as rated for Class A, B, C, or D fires.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Class of Fire/Type of Extinguisher chart (Figure 2.21)

question: According to the class-of-fire/extinguisher-type table, which extinguisher type is specifically listed for Class D fires (in addition to Multi-Purpose Dry Chemical)?
choice_a: Water, Loaded Steam Style
choice_b: Purple K Dry Chemical
choice_c: Water
choice_d: Foam
explanation: The table lists Purple K Dry Chemical as an extinguisher type rated for Class D fires.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Class of Fire/Type of Extinguisher chart (Figure 2.21)

question: According to the class-of-fire/extinguisher-type table, what type of extinguisher is Water With Anti-Freeze rated for?
choice_a: Class B or C
choice_b: Class A
choice_c: Class D
choice_d: Class A, B, C, or D
explanation: The table lists Water With Anti-Freeze as rated for Class A fires.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Class of Fire/Type of Extinguisher chart (Figure 2.21)

question: According to the class-of-fire/extinguisher-type table, Foam is listed as an extinguisher for which class(es) of fire?
choice_a: Class D only
choice_b: Class A, B, C, and D equally
choice_c: Class B, and on some Class A
choice_d: Class C only
explanation: The table lists Foam as rated for Class B, on some Class A fires.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, Class of Fire/Type of Extinguisher chart (Figure 2.21)

question: According to the manual, how many deaths per year result from traffic accidents involving people who drink alcohol?
choice_a: Over 5,000
choice_c: Over 50,000
choice_d: Over 20,000
explanation: People who drink alcohol are involved in traffic accidents resulting in over 20,000 deaths every year.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: What does alcohol impair, according to the manual?
choice_a: Muscle coordination, reaction time, depth perception, and night vision
choice_b: Only eyesight, and nothing else
choice_c: Only reaction time, and nothing else
choice_d: Only hearing
explanation: Alcohol impairs muscle coordination, reaction time, depth perception, and night vision. It also affects the parts of the brain that control judgment and inhibition.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: For some people, how many drinks does it take to show signs of impairment?
choice_a: One drink
choice_b: Five drinks
choice_c: Three drinks
choice_d: Impairment never begins below the legal limit
explanation: For some people, one drink is all it takes to show signs of impairment.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: How does alcohol travel through the body?
choice_a: It goes directly into the blood stream and is carried to the brain; a small percentage is removed through urine, perspiration, and breathing, while the rest is carried to the liver
choice_b: It is filtered out by the kidneys before reaching the bloodstream
choice_c: It is fully digested in the stomach and never reaches the brain
choice_d: It only affects the muscles, not the brain
explanation: Alcohol goes directly into the blood stream and is carried to the brain. After passing through the brain, a small percentage is removed in urine, perspiration, and by breathing, while the rest is carried to the liver.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: How much alcohol can the liver process per hour, according to the manual?
choice_a: Two ounces
choice_b: Only one-third an ounce
choice_c: There is no limit to how fast the liver processes alcohol
choice_d: A full ounce
explanation: The liver can only process one-third an ounce of alcohol per hour, which is considerably less than the alcohol in a standard drink.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: What does the manual say will sober you up after drinking?
choice_a: A cold shower
choice_b: Only time, not black coffee or a cold shower
choice_c: Vigorous exercise
choice_d: Black coffee
explanation: The liver processes alcohol at a fixed rate, so only time, not black coffee or a cold shower, will sober you up.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: What does BAC stand for and what does it measure?
choice_a: Braking Ability Coefficient, a vehicle performance rating
choice_b: Blood Alcohol Concentration, which commonly measures the amount of alcohol in your body
choice_c: Basic Accident Classification, a police reporting code
choice_d: Blood Acidity Content, a medical diagnostic measure
explanation: The Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) commonly measures the amount of alcohol in your body.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: Which three drinks does the manual say contain the same amount of alcohol?
choice_a: Any drink is equivalent regardless of size or proof
choice_b: A 16-ounce beer, an 8-ounce glass of wine, and a 2-ounce shot of liquor
choice_c: A 12-ounce glass of 5% beer, a 5-ounce glass of 12% wine, and a 1 1/2-ounce shot of 80 proof liquor
choice_d: A 6-ounce beer, a 4-ounce glass of wine, and a 1-ounce shot of liquor
explanation: The manual states a 12-ounce glass of 5% beer, a 5-ounce glass of 12% wine, and a 1 1/2-ounce shot of 80 proof liquor all contain the same amount of alcohol.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: What three factors determine Blood Alcohol Concentration, according to the manual?
choice_a: The amount of alcohol you drink, how fast you drink it, and your weight
choice_b: Your height, your gender, and the room temperature
choice_c: The brand of alcohol, the price paid, and the location
choice_d: The time of day, the type of glass used, and your age
explanation: BAC is determined by the amount of alcohol you drink (more alcohol means higher BAC), how fast you drink (faster drinking means higher BAC), and your weight (a small person doesn't have to drink as much to reach the same BAC).
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: Which part of the brain does alcohol affect first as BAC builds up?
choice_a: The part that controls breathing only
choice_b: The part that controls hearing
choice_c: The part that controls judgment and self-control
choice_d: The part that controls digestion
explanation: The first part of the brain affected controls judgment and self-control; one of the bad things about this is it can keep drinkers from knowing they are getting drunk.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: Which of the following is listed as an effect of alcohol on driving?
choice_a: Faster reaction time
choice_b: Straddling lanes and quick, jerky starts
choice_c: Better depth perception
choice_d: Improved night vision
explanation: Effects on driving may include straddling lanes and quick, jerky starts, among other errors.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: According to accident statistics cited in the manual, how does crash risk compare between drivers who have been drinking and those who have not?
choice_a: Drivers who have been drinking actually have a lower crash rate
choice_b: The chance of a crash is much greater for drivers who have been drinking
choice_c: The statistics are inconclusive
choice_d: There is no measurable difference
explanation: Accident statistics show that the chance of a crash is much greater for drivers who have been drinking than for drivers who have not.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving

question: According to the BAC effects chart, what happens at a BAC of .08?
choice_a: A mellow feeling with slight body warmth only
choice_b: Breathing stops
choice_c: Definite impairment in coordination and judgment; this is the drunk driving limit
choice_d: No noticeable effect
explanation: The BAC effects chart shows that at .08, there is definite impairment in coordination and judgment, described as the drunk driving limit with impaired coordination and judgment.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving, Effects of Increasing Blood Alcohol Content chart (Figure 2.23)

question: According to the BAC effects chart, at what level are people described as "clearly drunk" and "unable to drive"?
explanation: At .15, the chart shows impaired balance and movement, clearly drunk, and unable to drive.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving, Effects of Increasing Blood Alcohol Content chart (Figure 2.23)

question: According to the BAC effects chart, at what level does "coordination impairment" begin, alongside noticeable relaxation and being less alert?
explanation: At .05, the chart shows noticeable relaxation, and driving conditions show the driver is less alert, less self-focused, and coordination impairment begins.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving, Effects of Increasing Blood Alcohol Content chart (Figure 2.23)
