question: According to the BAC effects chart, at what level do many people lose consciousness?
explanation: At .30, the chart shows that many people lose consciousness.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving, Effects of Increasing Blood Alcohol Content chart (Figure 2.23)

question: According to the BAC effects chart, what happens at a BAC of .50?
choice_a: Mellow feeling with slight body warmth
choice_b: Breathing stops, and many die
choice_c: Noisy, possibly embarrassing behavior
choice_d: Definite impairment in coordination and judgment
explanation: At .50, the chart shows breathing stops and many die.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving, Effects of Increasing Blood Alcohol Content chart (Figure 2.23)

question: What does a BAC of .10 mean in terms of blood content?
choice_a: That your reaction time has improved by 10%
choice_b: That 10% of your total blood volume is alcohol
choice_c: That you have consumed exactly 10 drinks
choice_d: That 1/10 of 1% (or 1/1000) of your total blood content is alcohol
explanation: BAC of .10 means that 1/10 of 1% (or 1/1000) of your total blood content is alcohol.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving, Effects of Increasing Blood Alcohol Content chart (Figure 2.23)

question: About how often can the liver handle one drink, according to the discussion of increasing BAC?
choice_a: About five drinks per hour
choice_b: About one drink per day
choice_c: There is no limit; the liver processes alcohol instantly
choice_d: About one drink per hour, with the rest building up in your blood
explanation: Your BAC depends on the amount of blood and the amount of alcohol you consume over time; the faster you drink, the higher your BAC, as the liver can only handle about one drink per hour -- the rest builds up in your blood.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.1 Alcohol and Driving, Effects of Increasing Blood Alcohol Content

question: Which category of drugs does the manual specifically mention, including "pep pills," "uppers," and "bennies"?
choice_a: Amphetamines
choice_b: Antibiotics
choice_c: Antihistamines
choice_d: Antacids
explanation: Laws prohibit being under the influence of any controlled substance, amphetamines (including "pep pills," "uppers," and "bennies"), narcotics, or any other substance which can make the driver unsafe.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.2 Other Drugs

question: What kinds of legal drugs are noted as potentially unsafe if they make a driver drowsy?
choice_a: A variety of prescription and over-the-counter drugs, including cold medicines
choice_b: Only alcohol
choice_c: Only illegal narcotics
choice_d: Vitamins and supplements
explanation: This could include a variety of prescription and over-the-counter drugs (cold medicines), which may make the driver drowsy or otherwise affect safe driving ability.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.2 Other Drugs

question: When is possession and use of a doctor-prescribed drug permitted for a driver?
choice_a: Only during off-duty hours
choice_b: If the doctor informs the driver that it will not affect safe driving ability
choice_c: Only if it is an over-the-counter drug
choice_d: Never, regardless of doctor's orders
explanation: Possession and use of a drug given to a driver by a doctor is permitted if the doctor informs the driver that it will not affect safe driving ability.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.2 Other Drugs

question: What does the manual say is the only cure for fatigue, warning drivers not to use a drug that hides it?
choice_a: Caffeine
choice_b: Rest
choice_c: Cold water
choice_d: Exercise
explanation: Don't use any drug that hides fatigue -- the only cure for fatigue is rest.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.2 Other Drugs

question: How does alcohol interact with other drugs, according to the manual?
choice_a: Alcohol can make the effects of other drugs much worse
choice_b: Alcohol only affects the drugs it is chemically similar to
choice_c: Alcohol cancels out the effects of other drugs
choice_d: Alcohol has no interaction with other drugs
explanation: Alcohol can make the effects of other drugs much worse. The safest rule is don't mix drugs with driving at all.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.2 Other Drugs

question: What are some consequences of drug use leading to traffic accidents, according to the manual?
choice_a: No real consequences if no one is hurt
choice_b: Death, injury, property damage, arrest, fines, jail sentences, and the end of a driving career
choice_c: A temporary suspension of the CDL for one day
choice_d: Only a warning from police
explanation: Use of drugs can lead to traffic accidents resulting in death, injury, and property damage; it can also lead to arrest, fines, and jail sentences, and can mean the end of a person's driving career.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.2 Other Drugs

question: If you become too ill to operate a motor vehicle safely, what must you do?
choice_a: You may continue driving if the trip is short
choice_b: You must not drive
choice_c: You must drive only on local roads
choice_d: You must drive only at night
explanation: Once in a while, you may become so ill that you cannot operate a motor vehicle safely; if this happens, you must not drive.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.3 Illness

question: What is the one exception that allows a very ill driver to drive at all?
choice_a: You may always drive if you feel capable, regardless of illness
choice_b: You may drive if a passenger agrees to watch the road
choice_c: There is no exception; you must always stop immediately
choice_d: In case of an emergency, you may drive to the nearest place where you can safely stop
explanation: In case of an emergency, you may drive to the nearest place where you can safely stop.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.22.3 Illness

question: What must all drivers be able to do regarding hazardous cargo?
choice_a: Recognize hazardous cargo and know whether they can haul it without a hazardous materials endorsement
choice_b: Only drivers with a tank endorsement need this knowledge
choice_c: Nothing; hazmat rules apply only to dispatchers
choice_d: Only shippers need to know about hazardous materials, not drivers
explanation: All drivers should know something about hazardous materials. You must be able to recognize hazardous cargo, and you must know whether or not you can haul it without having a hazardous materials endorsement on your CDL license.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23 Hazardous Materials Rules For All Commercial Drivers

question: How does the manual define hazardous materials?
choice_a: Products that pose a risk to health, safety, and property during transportation
choice_b: Only liquids transported in bulk tanks
choice_c: Any cargo weighing more than 10,000 pounds
choice_d: Only products that are explosive
explanation: Hazardous materials are products that pose a risk to health, safety, and property during transportation.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.1 What Are Hazardous Materials?

question: What are the three intents of the rules about transporting hazardous materials?
choice_a: Track fuel usage, monitor engine health, and log driving hours
choice_b: Contain the product, communicate the risk, and ensure safe drivers and equipment
choice_c: Increase cargo capacity, reduce weight, and improve fuel economy
choice_d: Reduce shipping costs, speed up delivery, and simplify paperwork
explanation: The intent of the hazardous materials rules is to: contain the product, communicate the risk, and ensure safe drivers and equipment.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.2 Why Are There Rules?

question: How does the shipper communicate the risk of hazardous materials to dockworkers and drivers?
choice_a: Using a shipping paper and diamond shaped hazard labels
choice_b: By verbal notification only
choice_c: By requiring drivers to memorize a chemical list
choice_d: By painting the entire vehicle a warning color
explanation: To communicate the risk, the shipper uses a shipping paper and diamond shaped hazard labels to warn dockworkers and drivers of the risk.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.2 Why Are There Rules?

question: Why must a driver keep hazardous materials shipping papers identified or on top of other shipping papers?
choice_a: It has no safety purpose
choice_b: So firefighters and police can quickly locate them to know what hazardous materials are being transported after an accident or spill
choice_c: It is only a paperwork convenience for the shipper
choice_d: It speeds up loading time at the dock
explanation: After an accident or hazardous material spill or leak, you may be unable to communicate the hazards. Firefighters and police can prevent or reduce damage or injury if they know what hazardous materials are being transported, so you must identify or keep shipping papers related to hazmat on top of other shipping papers.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.2 Why Are There Rules?

question: Where must you keep hazardous materials shipping papers while driving?
choice_a: In a pouch on the driver's door, or in clear view within reach while driving
choice_b: In the glove compartment only, regardless of accessibility
choice_c: Mailed to the dispatch office
choice_d: In the trailer with the cargo
explanation: You must keep shipping papers in a pouch on the driver's door, or in clear view within reach while driving, or on the driver's seat when out of the vehicle.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.2 Why Are There Rules?

question: Where must you keep hazardous materials shipping papers when you are out of the vehicle?
choice_a: Locked in the trailer
choice_b: There is no requirement once you leave the vehicle
choice_c: In your personal bag
choice_d: On the driver's seat
explanation: Shipping papers must be kept on the driver's seat when out of the vehicle.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.2 Why Are There Rules?

question: What are placards, according to the manual?
choice_a: Signs put on the outside of a vehicle that identify the hazard class of the cargo
choice_b: Internal documents kept by the dispatcher only
choice_c: Labels used only for non-hazardous cargo
choice_d: Stickers placed only inside the cab
explanation: Placards are used to warn others of hazardous materials. Placards are signs put on the outside of a vehicle that identify the hazard class of the cargo.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products

question: How many identical placards must a placarded vehicle have, and where are they placed?
choice_a: At least four, placed on the front, rear, and both sides
choice_b: Six, one on each side of the vehicle and trailer
choice_c: Exactly one, placed on the rear only
choice_d: Only two, placed on the front and rear
explanation: A placarded vehicle must have at least four identical placards. They are put on the front, rear, and both sides.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products

question: What is the minimum required size of a placard, and what shape must it be?
choice_a: At least 20 inches square, in a rectangular shape
choice_b: At least 9.84 inches (250mm) square, turned upright on a point in a diamond shape
choice_c: There is no minimum size requirement
choice_d: At least 5 inches square, in a circular shape
explanation: Placards must be readable from all four directions and must be at least 9.84 inches (250mm) square, turned upright on a point, in a diamond shape.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products

question: What do cargo tanks and other bulk packaging display to identify their contents, besides placards?
choice_a: Only the shipper's company logo
choice_b: The identification number of their contents on placards or orange panels
choice_c: Nothing else is required beyond the placard color
choice_d: A photograph of the chemical
explanation: Cargo tanks and other bulk packaging display the identification number of their contents on placards or orange panels.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products

question: What are identification numbers used for, according to the manual?
choice_a: A tracking number used only by the shipping company's billing department
choice_b: The driver's CDL number
choice_c: A four digit code used by first responders to identify hazardous materials
choice_d: The vehicle's license plate number
explanation: Identification Numbers are a four digit code used by first responders to identify hazardous materials.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products

question: What letters precede a hazardous materials identification number?
choice_a: "HZ" or "DG"
choice_b: "US" or "DOT"
choice_c: "CDL" or "HM"
choice_d: "NA" or "UN"
explanation: The identification number will be preceded by the letters "NA" or "UN".
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products

question: What reference guide lists chemicals and their identification numbers, according to the manual?
choice_a: The vehicle owner's manual
choice_b: The US DOT Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)
choice_c: The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Handbook
choice_d: The CDL Skills Test Manual
explanation: The US DOT Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG) lists the chemicals and the identification numbers assigned to them.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products

question: Do all vehicles carrying hazardous materials need to have placards?
choice_a: Only vehicles carrying explosives need placards
choice_b: No, not all vehicles carrying hazardous materials need to have placards
choice_c: Placards are optional for all hazmat vehicles
choice_d: Yes, every vehicle carrying any amount of hazardous material must have placards
explanation: Not all vehicles carrying hazardous materials need to have placards; you can drive a vehicle that carries hazardous materials if it does not require placards.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products

question: If a vehicle requires placards, what must the driver have to legally drive it?
choice_a: Nothing extra; any CDL holder may drive it
choice_b: A note from the shipper only
choice_c: A driver license with the hazardous materials endorsement
choice_d: A general CDL with no endorsements
explanation: If a vehicle requires placards, you cannot drive it unless your driver license has the hazardous materials endorsement.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products

question: What must you do to get the hazardous materials endorsement?
choice_a: Pass only a driving skills test with no written component
choice_b: Simply request it when applying for a CDL, with no test
choice_c: Complete a one-day training course only
choice_d: Pass a written test on material found in Section 9 of the manual
explanation: To get the required endorsement, you must pass a written test on material found in Section 9 of this manual.

question: A tank endorsement is required for any commercial vehicle designed to transport liquid or gaseous materials in a tank with what individual rated capacity?
choice_a: More than 119 gallons
choice_b: More than 1,000 gallons
choice_c: More than 500 gallons
choice_d: More than 55 gallons
explanation: A tank endorsement is required for any commercial vehicle designed to transport liquid or gaseous materials in a tank or tanks having an individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate capacity of 1,000 gallons or more.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products

question: For the tank endorsement requirement, what is the minimum aggregate tank capacity that triggers the requirement?

choice_b: 1,000 gallons or more
choice_c: 500 gallons or more
choice_d: 119 gallons or more
explanation: The tank endorsement is required for tanks with an individual rated capacity of more than 119 gallons and an aggregate capacity of 1,000 gallons or more, permanently or temporarily attached to the vehicle or chassis.

question: If you don't know whether your vehicle needs placards, what should you do?

question: What does the manual say happens if you drive a vehicle needing placards without the hazardous materials endorsement, and get stopped?
choice_a: You only receive a warning the first time
choice_b: Only the shipper is held responsible, not the driver
choice_c: You will be cited and not allowed to drive your truck, costing time and money
choice_d: Nothing, as long as the cargo arrives safely
explanation: Never drive a vehicle needing placards unless you have the hazardous materials endorsement -- to do so is a crime. When stopped, you will be cited and you will not be allowed to drive your truck. It will cost you time and money.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products

question: What is the risk described if a driver fails to placard a vehicle when needed and is involved in an accident?

choice_b: There is no real risk beyond a fine
choice_c: It may risk the driver's life and others' lives because emergency help will not know of the hazardous cargo
choice_d: Only the vehicle's insurance is affected
explanation: A failure to placard when needed may risk your life and others if you have an accident, because emergency help will not know of your hazardous cargo.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.23.3 Lists of Regulated Products
